title: Tropical Storm Isaias Heads Toward the U.S. Gulf Coast
summary:
Tropical Storm Isaias formed on Wednesday in warm ocean water off eastern Mexico. Forecasters expect it to quickly grow stronger and become the first hurricane of this year's Atlantic season before it reaches the U.S. Gulf Coast. Landfall is expected late Friday or early Saturday, though the storm's path and timing could still shift.

Michael Brennan, director of the U.S. National Hurricane Center, said Isaias could become a major Category 3 hurricane, with winds of 178 kilometers per hour or stronger, before it reaches land. The center issued a hurricane watch for the northern Gulf Coast, from Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, to Indian Pass on the Florida Panhandle. A watch means hurricane conditions are possible within 48 hours. Forecasters also warned of storm surge, when ocean water is pushed onto land, and of heavy rain that could cause flash flooding near the coast.

Communities are preparing. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties. "While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously," Alabama Governor Kay Ivey wrote online. In Gulf Shores, Alabama, organizers canceled the National Shrimp Festival, which drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Some oil wells in the Gulf paused production, and eight of the Gulf's 371 staffed oil platforms were evacuated.

The storm might also disrupt Saturday's college football game between rivals Georgia and Alabama, which President Donald Trump has planned to attend.

This Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet because a strong El Niño has disrupted storm formation over that ocean. If Isaias becomes a hurricane, it could tie or break a 121-year-old record for the latest first hurricane of an Atlantic season. That record dates to 1905, when the year's first Atlantic hurricane formed on October 8.
why_it_matters: Hurricane forecasts and early warnings give families, schools and businesses time to prepare and stay safe. The storm also shows how ocean patterns like El Niño can shape weather far away.

background_read: A hurricane is a powerful storm that forms over warm ocean water and has strong winds spinning around a calm center called the eye.
Storms start out as tropical storms and are called hurricanes once their winds become strong enough.
The Atlantic hurricane season covers the months when these storms are most likely to form in the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf.
Forecasters at the U.S. National Hurricane Center track storms and issue watches and warnings so communities have time to prepare.
